payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
There is a serious argument circulating that friction in music-making is worth protecting, and that not every obstacle in a session is waste. Anyone who has lost two hours to a ground loop and come back to find the arrangement problem solved has met the version of it that is hard to dismiss. Music-making is an identity-forming process, and tools sold on speed and reduction of effort do miss most of what musicians value about it.

The argument is sound. It is also the one most likely to be borrowed by people whose product is a form.

The taxonomy already answers it

Friction in a studio comes in at least four kinds, and they are not interchangeable. Administrative friction is repetitive technical work. Creative friction is the doubting, failing, revising, and slow business of learning to recognize when something matters. Collaborative friction is latency and clock drift between musicians playing at a distance. Workflow friction is what the surrounding systems impose: licensing problems, broken or missing metadata, format incompatibility, rights and credits information that fails to travel.

A · Creative friction

Produces judgment

Doubting, failing, revising, learning to hear when something matters. Remove it and the process that makes a musician goes with it.

B · Workflow friction

Produces a completed field

Broken metadata, licensing problems, credits that fail to travel. Reducing it returns time and costs the work nothing.

Credits and rights information sit under workflow. Reducing that category does not diminish creative agency, and done well it returns time to the people doing the work. That settles the question the friction argument appears to open. Nobody has ever discovered their taste by re-entering a contributor name at a distributor that already received it from the studio.

What the interruption produces

Inconvenience is not the test. Creative friction earns its place by producing something: a decision that would not otherwise have been made, or an hour of not-thinking during which the problem solves itself. The output is judgment, and it belongs to the person who did the work.

A dialog asking a contributor to confirm their identity before bouncing a stem produces a completed field. It stops the work at the same cost in attention and returns nothing that was not already known before the interruption.

The field is thin in the other direction too. A declaration that costs nothing to enter and requires nothing to support it is worth about what an unsupported declaration is worth, which is why a blank and an honest answer end up in nearly the same place.

Who ends up paying

Sort the population by who has time. A studio with an assistant and a session administrator will produce complete records, because somebody is employed to produce them. A person finishing a mix alone at two in the morning, for a client who needed it yesterday, will not. The labor lands hardest on the contributors whose claims are weakest and who have the least ability to reconstruct anything later.

DDEX publishes a standard for exactly this. RIN captures contributor data in the studio and was designed to be built into recording software. Adoption is voluntary.

So the design constraint is not a preference about elegance. A record made by hand is a record made by the people who have staff. The only version that reaches everyone else accrues while the work is happening, asks for no confirmation, and is finished before anyone notices it started.

What that leaves unsettled is the part nobody has costed. A record that asks for nothing also cannot ask whether the person wanted to make it.

References

DDEX. Recording Information Notification (RIN). Current version 2.1. kb.ddex.net
